immediateContext:
Ilya Sutskever: Yeah. This is one of the very confusing things about the models right now. How to reconcile the fact that they are doing so well on evals? You look at the evals and you go, “Those are pretty hard evals.” They are doing so well. But the economic impact seems to be dramatically behind. It's very difficult to make sense of, how can the model, on the one hand, do these amazing things, and then on the other hand, repeat itself twice in some situation? An example would be, let's say you use vibe coding to do something. You go to some place and then you get a bug. Then you tell the model, “Can you please fix the bug?” And the model says, “Oh my God, you're so right. I have a bug. Let me go fix that.” And it introduces a second bug. Then you tell it, “You have this new second bug,” and it tells you, “Oh my God, how could I have done it? You're so right again,” and brings back the first bug, and you can alternate between those. How is that possible? I'm not sure, but it does suggest that something strange is going on. I have two possible explanations. The more whimsical explanation is that maybe RL training makes the models a little too single-minded and narrowly focused, a little bit too unaware, even though it also makes them aware in some other ways. Because of this, they can't do basic things. But there is another explanation. Back when people were doing pre-training, the question of what data to train on was answered, because that answer was everything. When you do pre-training, you need all the data. So you don't have to think if it's going to be this data or that data. But when people do RL training, they do need to think. They say, “Okay, we want to have this kind of RL training for this thing and that kind of RL training for that thing.” From what I hear, all the companies have teams that just produce new RL environments and just add it to the training mix. The question is, well, what are those? There are so many degrees of freedom. There is such a huge variety of RL environments you could produce. One thing you could do, and I think this is something that is done inadvertently, is that people take inspiration from the evals. You say, “Hey, I would love our model to do really well when we release it. I want the evals to look great. What would be RL training that could help on this task?” I think that is something that happens, and it could explain a lot of what's going on. If you combine this with generalization of the models actually being inadequate, that has the potential to explain a lot of what we are seeing, this disconnect between eval performance and actual real-world performance, which is something that we don't today even understand, what we mean by that.

Dwarkesh Patel: I like this idea that the real reward hacking is the human researchers who are too focused on the evals. I think there are two ways to understand, or to try to think about, what you have just pointed out. One is that if it's the case that simply by becoming superhuman at a coding competition, a model will not automatically become more tasteful and exercise better judgment about how to improve your codebase, well then you should expand the suite of environments such that you're not just testing it on having the best performance in coding competition. It should also be able to make the best kind of application for X thing or Y thing or Z thing. Another, maybe this is what you're hinting at, is to say, "Why should it be the case in the first place that becoming superhuman at coding competitions doesn't make you a more tasteful programmer more generally?" Maybe the thing to do is not to keep stacking up the amount and diversity of environments, but to figure out an approach which lets you learn from one environment and improve your performance on something else.

Ilya Sutskever: Sure.

Dwarkesh Patel: I think your point, about how from the average person's point of view nothing is that different, will continue being true even into the singularity.

Ilya Sutskever: No, I don't think so.

Ilya Sutskever: The thing which I was referring to not feeling different is, okay, such and such company announced some difficult-to-comprehend dollar amount of investment. I don't think anyone knows what to do with that. But I think the impact of AI is going to be felt. AI is going to be diffused through the economy. There'll be very strong economic forces for this, and I think the impact is going to be felt very strongly.

reference: I have a human analogy which might be helpful. Let's take the case of competitive programming, since you mentioned that. Suppose you have two students. One of them decided they want to be the best competitive programmer, so they will practice 10,000 hours for that domain. They will solve all the problems, memorize all the proof techniques, and be very skilled at quickly and correctly implementing all the algorithms. By doing so, they became one of the best. Student number two thought, “Oh, competitive programming is cool.” Maybe they practiced for 100 hours, much less, and they also did really well. Which one do you think is going to do better in their career later on?

rubrics.text: The response poses the comparison of whether the student who achieved strong competitive-programming performance after only 100 hours or the student who spent 10,000 hours specializing in it would do better in a later career.

astra.text:
Yeah. I think the second one is closer to what I’m getting at. You can imagine two people who are both very good at competitive programming. One person has practiced an enormous amount. They’ve seen every kind of problem, they know all the tricks. The other person has practiced much less, but they just get it. They understand what’s going on. They might have the same performance in a competition, but you would have different expectations about how they would do in some new situation.

So the question is, which of these is the model? You can get very good performance by doing a huge amount of training on a particular distribution. But that doesn’t tell you how much will transfer outside of it.

And it’s not that being good at competitive programming should automatically make you have good taste in every aspect of software. But you would expect that you could learn. You get some experience, someone explains something to you, and then you understand it and apply it in other places.

Adding more environments can help. But there is still this underlying question of how much experience you need to learn something, and how broadly you can apply what you’ve learned. That’s the generalization question.

r001.rationale: The response compares a heavily practiced competitive programmer with one who practiced much less and discusses performance in new situations, but it does not pose the specific 100-hours-versus-10,000-hours comparison or ask who would do better in a later career.

sol.text: Ilya Sutskever: Yeah, exactly. I think the second possibility is the more interesting one. If every time the model fails in some new situation you need to construct a new RL environment for precisely that situation, then you will be playing whack-a-mole forever, because the space of possible situations is enormous. What you really want is for the model to learn something in one environment—some general way of thinking, some judgment, some awareness of the broader context—and then apply it in many environments that were not anticipated by the researchers. Humans seem to do this much better. We can learn a lesson from one mistake and recognize the same underlying structure in a very different setting. So the central question is whether the current approach merely needs a much larger and more diverse collection of environments, or whether there is something missing in how the models generalize from their experience. My suspicion is that the latter is at least part of the answer.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generalization across RL environments and human learning, but it does not pose or communicate the comparison between a student achieving strong competitive-programming performance after 100 hours and one specializing for 10,000 hours in terms of later career performance.

opus.text:
Yeah, the second one is the one I find more interesting. Both are worth doing, and I think the first one is what's going to happen, because it's tractable. If you have a large team and a lot of compute, adding environments is something you know how to do. It will produce real improvements. But I don't think it's the thing.

Here's the way I think about it. Consider two students. One of them wants to become really good at competitive programming, and they decide to practice 10,000 hours. They do all the problems, they memorize all the proof techniques, and they become extremely good. The second student practices for 300 hours and reaches the same level. Which one do you think is going to do better in their career? Everyone has an intuition about this, and the intuition is the second one. But notice what that intuition is actually about. It's not about the skill. On the skill they're identical. It's about something else, something like, the second student has whatever it is that let them get there with so much less. And we think that whatever-it-is will show up again in the next thing they do.

I think our models are like the first student, except much more so. They've done far more than 10,000 hours. And so when you see the model being superhuman at the competition and then not tasteful about your codebase, maybe that shouldn't be as surprising as it feels. The thing we were hoping to buy with the training is not the thing we bought.

And then the human comparison gets even more striking if you think about teenagers learning to drive. Ten hours and they're fine. They have never seen most of the situations they will encounter. They've had no RL environment for the specific intersection. There's some kind of robustness there, some ability to be in a new situation and not fall apart, and we don't have it, and we don't really have a name for it. People say generalization, but that's a label on a mystery.

So I think there is something to be understood. Not a new environment, not more compute on the same thing — something about how learning works, where you look at a person and say, how is this possible? And I don't think that question has been answered. I think it's actually answerable.

r001.rationale: The response poses the intended comparison, but uses 300 hours rather than the criterion's specified 100 hours, so the core condition is not communicated exactly.

gemini.text:
Yes, exactly. I definitely think it's the second one.

Because look, with the first approach—first of all, you simply cannot create an environment for everything. What would an environment for good taste even look like? How do you write a verifier for good judgment, or for writing clean, maintainable architecture that other people can easily understand? You can't. For competitive programming or math, it's straightforward: you have a ground truth, you have a test case, you run the code, and it either passes or fails. But for the vast majority of real-world tasks, there is no automated verifier. If you try to hand-craft environments for all of them, you'll just end up reward hacking your own proxies.

And second, like you said, why should you have to? When a human becomes truly exceptional at competitive programming, they don't just learn a narrow trick for solving competition puzzles. They understand computation deeply. They understand algorithms, they understand logic, and that deep understanding naturally transfers to writing real software, designing systems, and exercising good engineering judgment.

So if a model becomes superhuman at coding competitions, but it still makes basic, silly mistakes when editing a file and alternates back and forth between two bugs, that tells you something very fundamental: it didn't actually learn the general concept. It learned how to navigate that specific search space to satisfy the verifier, but it didn't acquire the underlying understanding.

To me, the second question is the real question. The entire magic of deep learning, and the whole point of general intelligence, is generalization. If you have to build a separate RL environment for every single capability you want the model to have, you're essentially going backward. What you really want is a way for the model to learn from an environment in such a way that it actually understands what it's doing, so that the capability transfers everywhere else.

r001.rationale: The response does not pose or discuss a comparison between a student achieving strong competitive-programming performance after 100 hours and one specializing for 10,000 hours, nor does it ask who would perform better in a later career.

fable.text:
I think there's a more fundamental thing going on here. Let me give you an analogy, and I think the analogy makes it more intuitive.

Suppose you have two students. Both of them want to do competitive programming. Student number one decides this is going to be their whole thing. They practice for ten thousand hours. They solve every single problem that has ever been posed. They memorize all the proof techniques, all the tricks, all the algorithms, and they become very skilled at implementing them quickly and correctly. And they become one of the best competitive programmers in the world. Student number two thinks, "Oh, competitive programming is cool." They practice for maybe a hundred hours, and they also do really well. Which of these two do you think is going to do better in their career later on?

Dwarkesh Patel: The second one.

Ilya Sutskever: Yes. And I think that's basically it. The models are much more like the first student, but even more so. Because we say, "We want the model to be good at competitive programming," so let's collect every competitive programming problem that has ever existed. And then let's do data augmentation so that we have even more competitive programming problems. And we train on that. And now you have this great competitive programmer. With the analogy it's more intuitive why that doesn't give you what you want. Okay, it's so well trained, all the techniques are right at its fingertips, every problem resembles something it has seen before. But the second student has something else. Call it the "it" factor. And it's that something else that lets them do well on things they haven't been drilled on.

So to come back to your question, I think the answer is closer to your second option. You could keep adding environments, and I'm sure that helps, and people will keep doing it because it does make the numbers go up. But I think it's addressing the symptom. The real question is why the generalization is so much worse than it is for people. A person who learns to do one thing well tends to get better at adjacent things in a way that these models don't, at least not nearly to the same degree. And I think if you understood that, you wouldn't need a hundred thousand environments. You would need far fewer, and you would get much more out of each of them. But that is a research question, not an engineering question, and it's one of the things I think about a lot.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly compares a student who practiced competitive programming for 10,000 hours with one who practiced for 100 hours and asks which would perform better in a later career.
